transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-12
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Starlight CTO), Priya Rao (Starlight Head of ML), Aaron Choi (Starlight SRE)

Summary: POC scoping focused on cost modeling / unit economics for a customer pilot. Discussed target success criteria (latency/quality/cost), workload sizing, batching and caching knobs, and a benchmark plan. Agreed next steps to share cost spreadsheet and run a benchmark on dedicated hardware.

Topics: POC success criteria; per-token cost estimates; batching and KV/prefix caching; model size tradeoffs (13B vs 33B); timeline for benchmark and data sharing; security/VPC questions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE. We want to scope the POC today — especially the cost modeling side, the unit economics, and what success looks like. Maya is our SE and she'll drive the benchmark plan.
[00:18] Carlos: Thanks Jordan. Quick context — Starlight's chat assistant runs about 2.5M user requests a month, roughly 8M tokens/day during peak, but for the pilot we expect a narrower slice, maybe 500k tokens/day. Main asks are: parity with current quality, p50 latency <= 200ms, and keep incremental inference cost below $0.02 per 1k tokens if possible.
[00:38] Maya: cool, thanks. When you say "parity" — is that human eval pass rate or exact metric?
[00:45] Priya: we have an internal eval set, BLEU-ish style plus human A/B tests. For POC we want the model to match or beat our current 13B finetuned baseline on key prompts.
[00:55] Aaron: and from infra perspective we care about tail latency and predictable costs — need to model batching impact and peak capacity. Also VPC peering and egress limits matter if we go private.
[01:10] Jordan: noted. On the cost model front, there are two levers we'll quantify: the modeling cost per token (influenced by model size and quantization) and the system-level savings from batching and KV/prefix caching. We'll walk through ballpark per-token estimates and then propose a benchmark to validate.
[01:30] Maya: quick reality check — our typical per-token compute for a 13B on A100-ish hardware is X, and for 33B it's roughly 2.2x-2.5x depending on sequence length and quantization. We can run aggressive int8 quant to reduce compute, but that can affect quality.
[01:50] Carlos: can you give a sample per-token number so we can sanity check against our finance model?
[01:55] Maya: very rough: hosted inference baseline for a 13B might be 0.6 to 1.0 micro $ per 1k tokens? sorry, my numbers are fuzzy on the call, but Jordan will send the spreadsheet. The important part is the relative ratios: 33B is ~2.3x compute. Batch sizes can drop per-token cost by ~20-40% for streaming-style workloads if latency SLO allows slight batching.
[02:25] Priya: when you say batching reduces cost, what's the latency tradeoff? Our p50 target is 200ms, p95 should be <600ms ideally.
[02:33] Maya: If you keep batch windows very small (e.g., 20-50ms) you get most batching benefit with minimal added latency. For chat workloads we often do dynamic batching — immediate dispatch for single-turn requests, and a 25ms window for bursty traffic. Also prefix/KV cache helps huge — for multi-turn chat, caching previous KV states reduces repeated compute almsot linearly for short turns.
[02:55] Aaron: KV cache — is that on the server side? Do you store per-user caches and what's the memory cost?
[03:02] Maya: yes, it's in the serving runtime. Memory footprint depends on sequence length and model size; for a 13B with 1024 context the per-session KV is modest but we can quantify. For pilot we'll estimate memory per session and plan host counts.
[03:18] Jordan: let's talk success criteria concretely: 1) quality: match current eval scores; 2) latency: p50 <= 200ms, p95 <= 600ms; 3) cost: incremental per-token cost not exceed $0.02 per 1k tokens for pilot traffic, with roadmap to 0.01 with batching/cache/quantization. Does that align?
[03:36] Carlos: yes that's a good starting point. Finance would like a model showing per-month cost across 0.5M, 2M, and 8M daily token scenarios.
[03:45] Jordan: we'll include that in the spreadsheet. We'll show compute cost, instance amortization (for Dedicated), storage/egress, and any software fees.
[03:55] Priya: on Dedicated vs Hosted — what are tradeoffs? We like predictability and lower variable cost at scale, but we may not have the ops headcount yet.
[04:05] Maya: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower per-token cost at scale because you reserve GPU pools; Hosted is faster to launch but unit cost is higher. For POC, we recommend starting hosted for speed or a small dedicated pool for a true representative benchmark. For the pilot, a 2-node A100 pool should replicate production latencies for 13B.
[04:28] Aaron: network/VPC question — if we move to Private, can you support our KMS/HSM for key management? We have strict egress policies.
[04:36] Jordan: yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS and on-prem options. We'll include SOC2 docs and an architecture note.
[04:45] Carlos: competitors — we looked at Anthropic and OpenAI managed endpoints; pricing there was higher per token but simpler ops. We want Redwood if the unit economics make sense.
[04:57] Maya: noted. We'll benchmark both 13B quantized and a 33B lightly quantized model so you can compare quality vs cost.
[05:05] Jordan: benchmark plan: customer shares sample prompt corpus and traffic profile (Priya/Aaron). Redwood SE will run a set of passes: latency-only run, throughput run with synthetic QPS to measure cost at scale, and quality eval run against your eval set. We'll return raw numbers and an actionable cost model.
[05:25] Priya: timeline? We need results before our product review on 6/30.
[05:30] Maya: we can run an initial bench by 6/20 if we get prompts and infra info this week. Jordan will send the spreadsheet today.
[05:37] Jordan: yep, I'll send the cost template & example per-token calc after the call.
[05:41] Carlos: what about caching knobs — are those automatic or do we tune them?
[05:45] Maya: there's both automatic heuristics and tunable knobs. For example: batch max latency window, max batch size, and KV cache TTL. Each will be included in the report with recommended settings for your workload. In practice we see 25-40% token cost reduction from caching for multi-turn chat.
[06:05] Aaron: any concerns about model regressions with aggressive quant?
[06:09] Priya: yes, we care. We'll require a few targeted hallucination and accuracy checks in the QA.
[06:14] Maya: we'll include quality reg tests and holdout prompts in the benchmark. For quant we usually test int8 and int4-ish profiles and show quality delta.
[06:22] Carlos: ok. Finance also wants an example monthly bill for 500k tokens/day. Can you run that in the spreadsheet?
[06:29] Jordan: yes — we'll show line items: compute, infra (reserved GPU if Dedicated), storage/egress, Redwood platform fee, plus estimated savings from caching/batching.
[06:40] Priya: one more — do you support canary rollouts / A/B for production? We would like to run a canary to validate quality in prod.
[06:47] Maya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, traffic splitting, and automatic fallback on error rates. We'll include that as a recommended deployment plan post-POC.
[06:58] Jordan: quick recap of next steps: (1) Jordan send cost spreadsheet and SOC2/security docs; (2) Priya/Aaron share prompt corpus and traffic profile; (3) Maya run bench and return numbers by 6/20; (4) align on Dedicated vs Hosted based on results.
[07:15] Carlos: agreed. Anything else?
[07:18] Aaron: I'll follow up on VPC peering constraints.
[07:21] Priya: I'll anonymize and upload eval set.
[07:24] Jordan: great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with attachments and a calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff.
